title: Fall Protection Through Each Stage of Residential Framing
summary: Falls are the leading cause of death for residential construction workers. OSHA requires fall protection at 6 feet or more, and the right method changes at each stage of the build.
talking_points: Fall protection is required when you work 6 feet or more above a lower level in residential construction. That means guardrails, safety nets, or a personal fall arrest system (PFAS).

Trusses: use a bracket scaffold, platform ladder, or step ladder for a stable work surface. A spreader can act as an anchor and spreads fall forces across several trusses. A qualified person must decide if the trusses can take the load.
Roof sheathing and roofing: use safety nets, bracket scaffolds, or anchors with retractable lifelines. Inspect reusable and permanent anchors before every use.
Foundation work: strap anchors can be looped over rebar or set into the concrete. Straps that were poured in concrete or shock loaded are usually not reusable. Follow the manufacturer's instructions.
Floors and subfloors: use a truss bracket anchor system, mobile scaffolds, or wall bracket scaffolds. Put guardrails around floor openings. Add toeboards to protect people below from falling objects.

Walls: raise walls with a crane, boom truck, forklift, or jacks so fewer workers are exposed to falls. Guardrails across window and door openings help. Do not reuse a strap anchor that was cut or nailed off unless the manufacturer refurbishes it.
Exterior and interior finishing: use aerial lifts, ladders, or pump jack scaffolds outside. Use guardrails with toeboards at stairways, landings, and window openings inside.
If ordinary fall protection is truly not workable or is more dangerous, the employer must use a written fall protection plan under 29 CFR 1926.502(k). Some states have extra rules.
site_hazards_to_check: Roof trusses or rafters with no stable place to tie off
Open floor edges, stairwells, and basement openings
Unguarded window and door openings in framed walls
Damaged, cut, or shock-loaded anchor straps
Scaffold brackets, pump jacks, or ladder jacks that are loose or overloaded
Workers at the roof edge with no guardrail, net, or lifeline
discussion_questions: At what height do we need fall protection on this house, and what are we using at this stage?
Where is our anchor point today, and who checked that it can hold a fall?
What is our plan if our normal fall protection will not work for a task?
